levels.title_hi: जाता था · जाती थी · जाते थे

items.pronunciation_notes: Three heavy syllables in a row, all with the same long aa: maiṁ jaa-taa thaa.
items.gloss_en: मैं and वह take the same past auxiliary

learn.title_en: In the past, the auxiliary stops caring who you are
learn.explanation_en: मैं जाता था and वह जाता था are identical apart from the pronoun. That is not a coincidence — it is the central fact about the past auxiliary. था, थी, थे and थीं split by gender and number, and person plays no part in choosing between them. Compare the present, where हूँ, है, हो and हैं split by person and ignore gender completely. The two auxiliary sets are organised on opposite principles, which is why the past feels easier: there are only four forms and three of your pronouns can share one.

examples.note: Said by a man. The auxiliary is the same one वह uses.
Different person, identical verb.

examples.english: I used to go to school
examples.note: A whole sentence, and only the pronoun distinguishes it from the third person.

common_error.why_en: थे is the masculine plural. One speaker is singular, so था — the auxiliary is counting, not identifying who is talking.

practice.prompt_en: Conjugate the verb for this subject.
practice.question: जाना · मैं · masculine · habitual past
practice.explanation_en: Masculine singular on both words, so जाता and था.

game.question_en: Which form belongs in the habitual present cell?
game.explanation_en: मैं जाता हूँ. The first is the same cell one column left, and the fourth is presumptive.

items.pronunciation_notes: Two long ii endings, and थी keeps the aspirated th: maiṁ jaa-tii thii.
items.gloss_en: gender is what moves the past auxiliary

learn.explanation_en: A woman says मैं जाती थी, and both words have changed. This is the mirror image of what happened in the present, where switching gender moved the participle and left हूँ alone. Here the auxiliary is one of the things gender controls, so it moves too. Put the four sentences side by side and the system is visible at a glance: मैं जाता हूँ, मैं जाती हूँ, मैं जाता था, मैं जाती थी. The present auxiliary held still across genders; the past one does not.

examples.note: Said by a woman — both words are feminine.
Person makes no difference in the past, so the verb is identical.
Another verb, and the same pair of feminine endings.

common_error.why_en: The auxiliary carries gender in the past. Making the participle feminine and leaving था masculine is the usual half-correction.

practice.prompt_en: Conjugate the verb for this subject.
practice.question: जाना · मैं · feminine · habitual past
practice.explanation_en: Feminine singular on both words: जाती and थी.

game.question_en: Which form belongs in the habitual present cell?
game.explanation_en: मैं जाती हूँ. The last one is past and perfective — I had gone.

items.pronunciation_notes: Three clear e sounds, and थे is short and unstressed: ve jaa-te the.

learn.explanation_en: वे जाते थे puts the masculine plural on both halves, and the two endings match because they are the same marked ending doing the same job. You have seen this shape three times now in three modules — बड़े लड़के, वे जाते हैं, and now वे जाते थे. The past auxiliary थे is the one form of होना that looks like a participle, which is convenient here and worth flagging: it is not agreeing with जाते, it is agreeing with वे, and the two just happen to land on the same ending.

examples.note: Masculine plural on both words.

examples.english: the boys used to go to school
examples.note: A plural noun subject, and the verb reads it.
रहना again, in the cell it turns up in most often.

common_error.why_en: Both words have to go plural. Leaving either one singular is the commonest slip in this cell.

practice.prompt_en: Conjugate the verb for this subject.
practice.question: जाना · वे · masculine plural · habitual past
practice.question_read_as: jaanaa · ve · masculine plural · habitual past
practice.explanation_en: Masculine plural gives जाते and थे.

game.question_en: Which form belongs in the habitual present cell?
game.explanation_en: वे जाते हैं. The second is perfective past — they had gone.

summary.recap_en: The past auxiliary splits by gender and number and ignores person entirely, which is the exact reverse of the present set. That is why मैं जाता था and वह जाता था are the same verb, while मैं जाता हूँ and वह जाता है are not.
summary.next_up_en: Next: the habitual past with तुम, आप and हम, and how to say that something did not use to happen.

levels.title_hi: आप रहते थे · मैं नहीं जाता था

items.pronunciation_notes: रहते flattens in speech to rah-te, with the middle vowel dropped.
items.gloss_en: आप takes the plural past auxiliary

learn.title_en: आप is plural in the past too
learn.explanation_en: आप takes थे, exactly as वे does, and the participle stays plural — because आप is grammatically plural in every construction Hindi has. That is now four separate places you have seen the same fact: आपके rather than आपका in Module 6, आप पढ़ते हैं in level four, and now आप रहते थे. If you are speaking to one woman politely, both words go feminine plural: आप रहती थीं. The politeness does not change the gender, only the number.

examples.note: Plural on both words, for one listener or several.

examples.english: where did you use to live?
examples.note: The polite past version of the question from level four.
Said to a woman — feminine participle, feminine plural auxiliary.

common_error.why_en: आप never takes singular agreement, however few people you are addressing.

practice.prompt_en: Conjugate the verb for this subject.
practice.question: रहना · आप · masculine · habitual past
practice.explanation_en: आप is plural, so रहते and थे. The third option is present rather than past.

game.question_en: Which form belongs in the habitual present cell?
game.explanation_en: आप रहते हैं — the same cell, one column to the right.

items.pronunciation_notes: The kh needs a genuine puff of air behind it: ham khaa-te the.
items.gloss_en: first person plural in the past

learn.title_en: हम, and the past table completed
learn.explanation_en: हम takes थे, and with that you have the whole past auxiliary table: था for masculine singular, थी for feminine singular, थे for masculine plural, थीं for feminine plural. Four forms, and they are the ones Module 5 already taught you as the past of होना — nothing has been added to them. Which means the entire habitual past cost you exactly one thing to learn: that the participle stays put and the auxiliary changes. Everything else you brought with you.

examples.note: Plural on both words.
A place word slots in without touching the verb.
बोलना, and the same pair of plural endings.

common_error.why_en: थीं is feminine plural, and it would need the participle खाती in front of it. The two halves must agree with each other.

practice.prompt_en: Conjugate the verb for this subject.
practice.question: खाना · हम · masculine · habitual past
practice.explanation_en: Masculine plural on both words gives खाते थे.

game.question_en: Which form belongs in the habitual present cell?

items.pronunciation_notes: नहीं is two syllables ending on a hum, and in fast speech it shortens towards nahiṁ.
items.gloss_en: negation sits in front of the verb

learn.title_en: नहीं goes before the verb, and nothing else moves
learn.explanation_en: To say a habit did not hold, put नहीं directly in front of the verb: मैं नहीं जाता था. The participle and the auxiliary are untouched, which makes this the cheapest piece of grammar in the module. One thing worth knowing early, though: in the habitual present, speakers very often drop the auxiliary after नहीं — मैं नहीं जाता is more natural than मैं नहीं जाता हूँ. In the past that does not happen, and था stays. So the negative present is shorter than you expect and the negative past is not.

examples.english: I did not use to go
examples.note: नहीं in front, and the verb unchanged behind it.

examples.english: she did not use to go
examples.note: The negation is indifferent to gender.
Present tense, and the auxiliary has been dropped — which is what speakers usually do.

common_error.why_en: नहीं comes before the whole verb, not inside it. Splitting the participle from its auxiliary sounds distinctly wrong.

practice.question: मैं जाता था · negative
practice.explanation_en: नहीं goes in front of the verb and the rest of the sentence is unchanged.

game.question_en: Which form belongs in the habitual past cell?
game.explanation_en: मैं नहीं जाता था. The first is habitual present with the auxiliary dropped, and the last is perfective.

summary.recap_en: The habitual past is complete. था, थी, थे and थीं are Module 5's past of होना, untouched, and नहीं placed in front of the verb negates any of them. In the habitual present the auxiliary is usually dropped after नहीं; in the past it is not.
summary.next_up_en: Next: the continuous, which is the cell English speakers reach for constantly and have been getting wrong since level two.

levels.title_hi: जा रहा हूँ · जा रही है · जा रहे हैं

items.pronunciation_notes: Three separate words, and रहा keeps its h audible as a breath: jaa ra-haa huuṁ.

learn.title_en: This is the one that means 'I am going'
learn.explanation_en: Level two warned you that मैं जाता हूँ is not I am going. This is the form that is. It has three pieces written as three words: the bare stem जा, the marker रहा, and the auxiliary हूँ. The stem is the verb with -ना stripped off and nothing added — not the participle, just the bare stem, which is a different base from the one the habitual uses. रहा is the piece that carries gender and number, and the auxiliary carries person, exactly as before. So the two agreements you already know are still running; they have just moved onto a different word.

examples.note: Right now, at this moment — not a habit.
The same sentence as level two, in the cell that actually means what English says.
पढ़ना gives the bare stem पढ़ — drop -ना and add nothing.

common_error.why_en: The continuous is built on the bare stem, never on the habitual participle. The two bases do not stack.

practice.prompt_en: Conjugate the verb for this subject.
practice.question: जाना · मैं · masculine · continuous present
practice.explanation_en: Bare stem जा, masculine singular marker रहा, and मैं takes हूँ.

game.question_en: Which form belongs in the continuous present cell?
game.explanation_en: मैं जा रहा हूँ. The first is habitual present, which is the pair worth keeping apart.

items.pronunciation_notes: रही holds a long ii at the end, which is the only thing separating it from रहा: ra-hii.

learn.title_en: रहा becomes रही, and nothing else does
learn.explanation_en: The marker takes the marked endings you have been using since Module 6: रहा for masculine singular, रही for anything feminine, रहे for masculine plural. It is the third word in a row that behaves this way — बड़ा, जाता, and now रहा — because all three are marked forms agreeing with the subject. Notice which word is doing the agreeing and which is not. जा never changes, in any cell, for any subject. The stem is inert; the marker carries everything.

examples.note: Feminine marker रही with the third person auxiliary.

examples.english: the girl is going to school
examples.note: A feminine noun subject, and the marker reads it.
Probably the most useful continuous question in the language.

common_error.why_en: Not ungrammatical, but it means he rather than she. वह is genderless, so the marker is the only thing telling your listener who you mean.

practice.prompt_en: Conjugate the verb for this subject.
practice.question: जाना · वह (feminine) · continuous present
practice.explanation_en: Feminine marker रही, and वह takes है.

game.question_en: Which form belongs in the habitual present cell?
game.explanation_en: वह जाती है. The first is the same column, one row up in aspect.

items.pronunciation_notes: रहे is short and unstressed, sitting between two longer words: ve jaa ra-he haiṁ.

learn.title_en: Three words, and only the middle one moves
learn.explanation_en: वे जा रहे हैं completes the set. Look at what has happened across these three items: जा has not changed once, रहा has taken all three marked endings, and the auxiliary has followed the person as it always does. That is the whole continuous. It looks harder than the habitual because it is three words instead of two, but there is genuinely less to decide — the habitual made you build a participle from the verb, and here the verb contributes a bare stem and then sits out.

examples.note: Masculine plural marker with the plural auxiliary.

examples.english: the boys are going to school
examples.note: A plural noun subject, and both agreeing words follow it.
करना gives the bare stem कर, and this question will come up constantly.

common_error.why_en: The marker has to go plural too. Fixing only the auxiliary is the same half-correction that showed up in the habitual.

practice.prompt_en: Conjugate the verb for this subject.
practice.question: जाना · वे · masculine plural · continuous present
practice.question_read_as: jaanaa · ve · masculine plural · continuous present
practice.explanation_en: Masculine plural marker रहे with the plural auxiliary हैं.

game.question_en: Which form belongs in the continuous present cell?
game.explanation_en: वे जा रहे हैं — bare stem plus marker plus auxiliary.

summary.recap_en: The continuous is bare stem plus रहा plus होना. The stem never changes for anyone; रहा takes the marked endings रहा, रही, रहे; the auxiliary follows the person. This is the cell that means what English -ing means, and it is the one to reach for when something is happening now.
summary.next_up_en: Next: the continuous with other verbs and other persons, including the question you will be asked more than any other.

levels.title_hi: क्या कर रहे हो? · पढ़ रही है

items.pronunciation_notes: क्या is one syllable, not two: kyaa, with the k and y run together.
items.gloss_en: the most-used continuous question in Hindi

learn.title_en: The question you will hear most
learn.explanation_en: तुम क्या कर रहे हो is what are you doing, and it is worth over-learning because it opens more Hindi conversations than any other sentence. Three things to notice. The bare stem of करना is कर, which is the verb with -ना removed and nothing else done to it. तुम takes रहे and हो, plural on both counts as always. And क्या sits in second position, before the verb — the question word slots in and the verb is completely unaffected by its presence.

examples.note: The casual register. Use आप with anyone you do not know.
The polite version, and the one to default to.
A different question word in the same slot, and the verb is unchanged.

common_error.why_en: करता is the habitual participle. The continuous needs the bare stem कर, with nothing added to it at all.

practice.prompt_en: Conjugate the verb for this subject.
practice.question: करना · तुम · continuous present
practice.explanation_en: तुम is plural, so रहे, and its auxiliary is हो.

game.question_en: Which form belongs in the habitual present cell?
game.explanation_en: तुम क्या करते हो — what do you do, as in for a living, rather than at this moment.

items.pronunciation_notes: बोल has a long open o and no vowel after the l: bol.

learn.title_en: Any verb, the same three pieces
learn.explanation_en: बोलना gives the stem बोल, and everything else is what you already have. That is the point of this item: there is no list of verbs that work differently in the continuous. Strip -ना, and whatever is left is the stem, for every verb in the language. Compare this with the habitual, where you still had to add -ता or -ती or -ते and choose correctly. The continuous asks the verb for less and asks रहा for more, which is why it tends to click faster than the habitual does.

examples.note: Bare stem बोल, plural marker, plural auxiliary.
खाना gives the stem खा — a long vowel, and nothing added.
रहना gives रह, which sits right next to the marker रहे and sounds odd at first.

common_error.why_en: बोलते is the habitual participle. Only the bare stem can carry the continuous marker.

practice.prompt_en: Conjugate the verb for this subject.
practice.question: बोलना · हम · masculine · continuous present
practice.explanation_en: Stem बोल, plural marker रहे, and हम takes हैं.

game.question_en: Which form belongs in the habitual present cell?
game.explanation_en: हम बोलते हैं — we speak Hindi, as a standing fact about us.

items.pronunciation_notes: पढ़ ends on a flapped ṛh with breath behind it, and no vowel follows: paṛh.
items.gloss_en: a transitive verb in the continuous, with no ने

learn.explanation_en: पढ़ना takes an object — you read something — and that makes it a transitive verb. In the continuous this changes absolutely nothing: the subject is plain लड़की, the object किताब sits in front of the verb, and the agreement still runs off the subject. It is worth saying now because Module 9 is going to introduce a construction where transitive verbs behave very differently, and learners often start applying it too early. The rule to hold: that construction belongs to the perfective only. Habitual and continuous never touch it, whatever the verb.

examples.english: the girl is reading a book
examples.note: The marker agrees with लड़की, the subject, not with किताब.

examples.english: the boy is reading a book
examples.note: Same object, and the marker has changed with the subject.
A plural subject and a singular object — the verb follows the subject.

common_error.why_en: The marker agrees with the subject लड़की, which is feminine. किताब being feminine too is a coincidence here and not the reason.

practice.prompt_en: Conjugate the verb for this subject.
practice.question: पढ़ना · लड़की · continuous present
practice.explanation_en: लड़की is feminine and singular, so रही and है.

game.question_en: Which form belongs in the habitual present cell?
game.explanation_en: लड़की किताब पढ़ती है — she reads books, rather than she is reading one now.

summary.recap_en: Every verb makes its continuous the same way: strip -ना and use what is left. Transitive verbs behave no differently — an object sits in front of the verb and the agreement still runs off the subject, which will stop being true in Module 9 but only for the perfective.
summary.next_up_en: Next: habitual against continuous, put side by side — and one verb whose stem collides with the marker.

items.pronunciation_notes: Two breathy sounds in a row, the ढ़ and the ह of रहा, and neither should be swallowed.
items.gloss_en: the minimal pair that carries the whole distinction

learn.title_en: वह पढ़ता है and वह पढ़ रहा है
learn.explanation_en: Same verb, same person, same time, and two completely different claims. वह पढ़ता है says he studies — he is a student, it is what he does. वह पढ़ रहा है says he is reading right now, and tells you nothing about whether he ever does it otherwise. English uses studies and is studying for exactly this split, so the distinction is not new to you; what is new is that Hindi will not let you blur it. There is no form that covers both, and choosing the habitual for a present moment is the error that marks a learner most audibly.

examples.note: Right now. Say nothing about his habits.
A fact about him. He may be asleep as you say it.
रोज़ can only go with the habitual, which is a useful test.

common_error.why_en: A word meaning right now cannot sit with the habitual. If the sentence points at this moment, the aspect has to be continuous.

practice.prompt_en: Conjugate the verb for this subject.
practice.question: पढ़ना · वह · masculine · continuous present
practice.explanation_en: Bare stem पढ़, masculine marker रहा, and वह takes है.

game.question_en: Which form belongs in the habitual present cell?
game.explanation_en: वह पढ़ता है. The four options are the four corners of the two aspects across two times.

items.pronunciation_notes: Two similar syllables back to back, and both need their h: rah ra-haa.
items.gloss_en: when the stem and the marker collide

learn.title_en: रह रहा — the one that sounds like a mistake
learn.explanation_en: रहना means to live or stay, and its bare stem is रह. Put it in the continuous and you get मैं रह रहा हूँ, with the stem sitting directly against the marker. Learners assume they have doubled a word by accident and delete one. They have not. The two are unrelated: रह is the verb, and रहा is the continuous marker, which happens to come from the same root historically but is doing an entirely different job here. The sentence is correct and common, and you will need it whenever you talk about where you are staying rather than where you live.

examples.note: Temporarily — the continuous makes it a current arrangement.

examples.hindi: मैं शहर में रह रहा हूँ
examples.read_as: maiṁ shahar meṁ rah rahaa huuṁ
examples.english: I am staying in the city
examples.note: शहर is oblique before में, and the verb is unaffected.
The habitual, which means the city is where you are from rather than where you happen to be.

common_error.why_en: Deleting what looks like a repeated word removes the verb and leaves only the marker. Both are needed.

practice.prompt_en: Conjugate the verb for this subject.
practice.question: रहना · मैं · masculine · continuous present
practice.explanation_en: Stem रह, marker रहा, auxiliary हूँ — three separate words that only look repetitive.

game.question_en: Which form belongs in the habitual present cell?
game.explanation_en: मैं रहता हूँ — where I live, rather than where I am currently staying.

tts_strings: मैं शहर में रह रहा हूँ

items.pronunciation_notes: The breathy ढ़ runs straight into रहा with no vowel between: paṛh ra-haa.
items.gloss_en: the two aspects, one after the other

learn.title_en: Asked about now, then asked about always
learn.explanation_en: Four lines and the aspect switches once, in the middle. The first question asks what is happening at this moment, so both speakers use the continuous. The third question adds रोज़ and asks about a habit, and both switch to the habitual — the verb is the same throughout, only the aspect moves. This is what the distinction sounds like when it is doing real work rather than sitting in a table. Notice too that the last line drops हिंदी: once it has been said, Hindi leaves it out rather than repeating it.

lines.speaker: A
lines.hindi: क्या तुम रोज़ हिंदी पढ़ते हो?
lines.read_as: kyaa tum roz hindii paṛhte ho?
lines.english: Do you study Hindi every day?

common_error.wrong: हाँ, मैं रोज़ पढ़ रहा हूँ।
common_error.why_en: रोज़ makes the sentence about a habit, and a habit cannot be expressed with the continuous.

practice.question: क्या तुम रोज़ हिंदी ___ हो?
practice.explanation_en: रोज़ forces the habitual, and तुम takes the plural participle पढ़ते.

game.question_en: Listen to the second line. Which word is missing?
game.explanation_en: A single male speaker, so the marker is रहा — and हूँ at the end confirms the number.

tts_strings: क्या तुम रोज़ हिंदी पढ़ते हो?

summary.recap_en: The habitual and the continuous are not interchangeable and Hindi offers no form that covers both. रोज़ can only go with the habitual and a word meaning now can only go with the continuous, which makes the adverb a reliable test when you are unsure which cell you need.
summary.next_up_en: Next: the continuous past, which is one word away from everything you just learnt.
